client: I've been really dreading this family reunion coming up next month. Ever since that big fight with my cousin last year, just thinking about seeing them again makes my chest feel tight and my heart pound. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help - I mean, the tension is already there, right?
therapist: I hear how much anxiety this reunion is stirring up for you, especially after that difficult conflict with your cousin. That physical tightness and pounding heart shows how deeply this situation is affecting you. What thoughts come up when you imagine walking into that reunion space?

client:
I keep imagining everyone staring at me when I walk in, judging me for what happened last time. My mind races with thoughts like "They all think I'm the problem" and "Why did I even agree to come?" It's like my body goes into panic mode before I'm even there. 

The worst part is that I know my cousin will probably act like nothing happened, which makes me even more anxious because I'm still so upset about it. I don't know how to act normal when I feel anything but normal about the situation.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is creating some very vivid and distressing predictions about how this reunion will go, which is understandably making you feel panicked. The contrast between your lingering hurt and the possibility of your cousin acting casually must feel especially difficult to navigate. What would it feel like to acknowledge that your reaction makes complete sense given what happened between you?

client:
It does make sense that I'm reacting this way, but that doesn't make the anxiety any easier to handle. I keep picturing walking into the reunion and my cousin just brushing me off like nothing happened, and it makes my chest feel tight. 

I know logically that my reaction is justified after how she ghosted me, but part of me still feels guilty for making such a big deal out of it when she might not even care.
therapist: I hear that painful conflict between your justified feelings and the guilt that comes up when you imagine her indifference. That tightness in your chest shows how much emotional weight this unresolved situation still carries for you. What would it feel like to give yourself permission to honor your feelings, regardless of how she chooses to act?

client:
I want to believe my feelings matter, but it's hard when she acts like they don't. Every time I try to honor my emotions, I just hear her voice in my head saying I'm being too sensitive. That makes the guilt come rushing back even stronger. 

Part of me knows you're right, but another part keeps thinking - what if she's right and I really am overreacting? The more I try to validate myself, the more confused I get.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a painful tug-of-war between trusting your own experience and absorbing her dismissive messages. That confusion makes complete sense when you've been told your feelings are "too much" - it can make reality feel shaky. What might it feel like to gently notice when her critical voice appears in your thoughts, and remind yourself that your emotions are always valid?

client: I get what you're saying about noticing the critical voice, but it's hard to separate it from my own thoughts sometimes. When I try to remind myself my feelings are valid, part of me just thinks "but what if she's right?" and then I feel even more confused. It's like my brain automatically believes her more than it believes me.
therapist: That struggle to distinguish between her voice and your own thoughts shows how deeply those dismissive messages have affected you. It makes sense that this creates confusion when your brain has learned to prioritize her perspective over your own truth. What might happen if you treated that doubting voice with curiosity rather than certainty when it arises?

client: I get what you're saying about treating the voice with curiosity, but it's hard because that voice feels so real in the moment. When I hear those dismissive thoughts, they immediately trigger this wave of anxiety that makes it hard to step back and question them. Part of me worries that if I don't take those thoughts seriously, I'll miss something important or make a mistake.
therapist: That immediate wave of anxiety makes it so difficult to create space between you and those thoughts - it's understandable why they feel so convincing in the moment. Your worry about missing something important shows how protective that anxious response is trying to be. What would it feel like to acknowledge both the protective intention behind those thoughts and your own wisdom in questioning them?

client:
I get what you're saying about the anxiety trying to protect me, but it's hard to see it that way when it just feels like my brain working against me. When the panic hits, all I can think is "something terrible is about to happen" - it doesn't feel protective, it feels like a warning I can't ignore. 

I do try to question the thoughts sometimes, but in the moment it's like my body reacts before my mind can catch up - my heart races and I can't think straight. How am I supposed to acknowledge the protective intention when it just feels like pure terror?
therapist: I hear how overwhelming and all-consuming that terror feels in your body when the panic hits - it makes complete sense that it doesn't feel protective when you're in the thick of it. That disconnect between your racing body and your thinking mind is exactly what makes anxiety so disorienting in the moment. What would it feel like to practice noticing those physical sensations with gentle curiosity when they arise, rather than needing to change them immediately?

client: I get what you're saying about noticing the sensations with curiosity, but when I'm in that panicked state, it feels impossible to be curious. My brain just screams that something is terribly wrong, and all I can think about is making it stop. Even the idea of trying to observe it makes me more anxious - like I'm just going to get sucked deeper into the panic.
therapist: I hear how terrifying and all-encompassing that panicked state feels - when your brain is screaming that something is wrong, any suggestion to observe it can understandably feel impossible or even dangerous. That fear of being pulled deeper into the panic shows just how intense and real this experience is for you. What would it feel like to acknowledge that right now, in this moment with me, you're actually already practicing being with these difficult feelings in a safer way?

client: I guess I never thought about it that way before - that just sitting here talking about it means I'm already facing the panic in a safer space. But part of me worries this is just temporary relief, you know? Like what if I leave this office and the anxiety comes back even stronger because I'm actually paying attention to it now?
therapist: That's such an understandable concern - the fear that paying attention might somehow "feed" the anxiety is very common when we start exploring these patterns. Yet what if this conversation is showing you that you can face these feelings without being overwhelmed by them? How might it feel to notice that you're already proving your anxiety wrong by having this conversation?

client: I guess that makes sense... but it still feels like I'm playing with fire when I focus on the anxiety. Like if I look at it too closely, it'll just grow bigger. I can talk about it now, but what if later tonight it comes back even worse? That's what usually happens.
therapist: I hear how scary that anticipation feels - like examining the anxiety might somehow give it more power over you later. Yet notice how right now, as we're talking about it, the anxiety hasn't actually overwhelmed you despite your fears. What would it be like to gently observe that difference between what you fear might happen and what's actually happening in this moment?
